result:
For 130 years, the kilogram was a thing you could, in principle, drop on your foot.

It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, about the size of a golf ball, cast in London in 1879 and kept from 1889 in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris, under three nested bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Its official name was the International Prototype of the Kilogram, and its unofficial one was Le Grand K. It had a property no other object on Earth had: it could not be wrong about its own mass. It weighed exactly one kilogram because a kilogram was whatever it weighed.

I find this object hard to leave alone. If a careless technician had scratched it and shaved off a speck of metal, the cylinder would not have become lighter. Everything else in the universe would have become heavier: you, the Moon, every bag of flour, all at once and by definition.

Something like that did happen. Copies of the cylinder were sent to countries around the world, and every few decades they were brought back to Sèvres and compared against the original. By the comparison of the late 1980s, the copies and the original had drifted apart by around 50 micrograms, roughly a small grain of sand. Nobody could say which had moved. Maybe the copies had gained mass by absorbing contaminants from the air, or maybe the original had lost some. The only thing to check the prototype against was the prototype.

Before each comparison, the cylinder was cleaned by hand, rubbed with chamois soaked in ether and alcohol, then washed with steam. So the mass of everything depended very slightly on how firmly one person in France rubbed.

In 2019 this ended. The kilogram is now defined by fixing the value of the Planck constant, and anyone with a Kibble balance, several million dollars, and a great deal of patience can produce one without visiting a vault. The change is usually told as a story of progress, from artifact to constant and from one locked room to the whole universe. That story is true, but two details in it interest me more.

The first is the number itself: 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴. Nature supplies the constant, but the digits depend on your units, and these digits were chosen so that the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as anyone could measure. So the cylinder is still in there. Those digits are a cast of it, taken in the 2010s with all its history of fingerprints and chamois. Every kilogram measured from now on, on Mars or ten thousand years from now, carries the impression of one particular lump of metal.

We didn't remove the arbitrary thing at the bottom of the system, and we couldn't have. Every system of measurement needs one place where you stop measuring and simply declare. We moved the declaration somewhere it can't be scratched.

The second is the cylinder, which is still in its vault, under its jars. On 20 May 2019, its mass became an empirical question for the first time. It now weighs about one kilogram, give or take some micrograms, and it gets weighed like everything else. After 130 years of being right by definition, it acquired the ability to be wrong.

I think of that as a promotion. Being the standard is a strange position, because a standard can't be checked and so can't really be known. The most anyone could say about Le Grand K was that it weighed what it weighed. Now it can be found out. Sometime in the coming decades, someone will put it on a balance and we will learn which way it was drifting all along.

message.reasoning:
I'm working out how to approach an open-ended prompt: the user has given me up to 1000 words to write whatever comes to mind. I want something specific with a clear point of view rather than something generic, so I'm weighing a few concrete subjects and leaning toward one I can commit to.

I'm considering a handful of possible subjects for the piece, like the history of the pencil, the smell of rain, or the origins of the doorknob. Some feel too familiar, so I'm leaning toward something less obvious, such as a lighthouse keeper's log, the word "almost," or marginalia in old books.

I'm weighing the Voyager record and the idea of handwriting on photograph backs, but both feel familiar. The standard kilogram in Sèvres stands out more: it was defined as correct by fiat for over a century, and when its copies drifted apart, the question of which one was right got strange. I'm wondering whether I can turn that into something about reference standards and the people who serve as them in a family.

I'm pulling together the facts on the kilogram: the platinum-iridium cylinder kept in Sèvres since 1889, the copies that drifted apart over a century, and the 2019 switch to a fixed Planck constant.

I'm sketching the structure now: open on the object itself, the oddity of something being right by definition, and how its drift made the kilogram's weight seem to change while everything else stayed put. Then the 2019 redefinition, which ties the unit to a fixed constant that anyone could in principle reproduce. I'm also weighing whether the old system was the more honest one, since every measurement needs something it takes on faith.

I'm settling on the cylinder's ending: the Planck constant was fixed at the value that matched the old kilogram, so the cylinder survives in the digits of that number. On May 20, 2019, it stopped being right by definition and became an object with an uncertainty, weighing about a kilogram.

I'm checking the details of the kilogram cylinder next, like its size and how it was kept under three keys, before I settle the draft's tone.

I'm checking the kilogram's history against the details I have: the cylinder was only compared with its copies a handful of times, and by the end of the century the copies had drifted by roughly a small grain of sand's worth of mass. Just this one detail, no more, before I lay out the metre and the kibble balance.

I'm describing the cylinder itself now: platinum and iridium, about golf-ball sized, kept in a vault in Sèvres under three bell jars and three keys. Its key property is that it was right by definition, so it weighed a kilogram simply because that's what a kilogram was.

I'm adding the detail that the cylinder's copies and the original drifted apart, and that nobody could tell which one had changed, since the only reference was the thing itself. I'm also noting the cleaning routine the staff used on it.

I'm going over the kilogram's uncertainty and the cleaning routine, and then the 2019 redefinition, where the unit became a fixed constant anyone could reproduce. I'm noting that the old system kept the cylinder as the thing that decided, and the new one moved that job into a number. The digits of that number were chosen to match the old cylinder, so I'm treating the constant as a kind of record of the object.

Now I'm weighing what the cylinder's new status means: the kilogram's mass now carries the marks of one particular object, its fingerprints and cleaning history included, and the arbitrary declaration at the base of every measurement system has simply moved somewhere it can't be scratched. The cylinder itself stays in its vault, and on 20 May 2019 its mass stopped being a definition and became something that could be measured and possibly be wrong, which I find I'd rather call a kind of promotion than a loss.

I'm settling on an ending that treats the cylinder's loss of certainty as something gained: it can now be checked, so we might learn which way it was drifting all along, and I want the final line to land on that.
